Nov 5 : Anthropic's AI models are improving nearly twice as fast as before as the technology plays a bigger role in developing more powerful versions of itself, an independent study found, fanning concerns that advances could outpace efforts to assess risks. The findings from AI safety nonprofit METR, published on Thursday, offer some of the clearest evidence yet that AI is accelerating its own development, potentially paving the way for recursive self-improvement (RSI), when AI systems can build more powerful versions of themselves without human intervention. METR estimated AI accounted for perhaps 80 per cent of the current acceleration, though it cautioned that the figure was uncertain. The researchers found no convincing evidence of major bottlenecks that could slow progress over the next year. "We are confident that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scaling of training compute," METR, also known Model Evaluation and Threat Research, said.

But it cautioned that AI was not yet capable of making highly significant, fully autonomous contributions to the most important stages of model training. The prospect of recursive self-improvement has fueled warnings from AI researchers in recent months that such systems could become difficult to align with human goals, monitor and control, potentially posing an existential threat to humanity. Such a shift could have far-reaching implications for an industry that has spent hundreds of billions of dollars building computing infrastructure to train advanced models as AI itself could become an important driver of technological progress. METR's 11-week assessment, which drew on confidential research, interviews and performance data from unreleased models, found Anthropic's benchmark capabilities had been improving 1.9 times faster since October 2025 than previously.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON, Nov 5 : The US Federal Aviation Administration said on Thursday it will replace by the end of 2028 the outdated floppy disks used for weather and other critical information at more than 400 air traffic control facilities across the country.  The Enterprise Information Display System will replace four systems dating back to the 1980s and will put important operational information in one place so controllers can quickly see air traffic updates. Floppy disks largely stopped being used more than 25 years ago and have not been produced in large numbers since 2011. Congress last year approved $12.5 billion to fix the aging US air traffic control system and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wants another $30 billion for additional upgrades as the FAA deals with numerous technology issues. “We’re moving away from outdated, manual processes and replacing technology that once relied on floppy disks with a modern system that allows controllers to instantly share critical flight alerts, restricted airspace schedules and pilot reports," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said in a statement.

In a previously unreported October 23 FAA memo to airports seen by Reuters, the agency said "there have been a number of recent air traffic control outages due to fiber optic cable cuts, which can lead to delays, diversions and cancellations" and urged coordination with the FAA on projects. The FAA cited an October 13 event where a fiber optic cable connecting Houston George Bush Intercontinental Airport to the FAA’s network was cut outside an airport gate, leading to the loss of data services between FAA facilities and requiring a ground stop. In September, thousands of flights across the densely populated Northeast were delayed or canceled due to the dual failures of a circuit at a Philadelphia air traffic facility and the accidental severing of a fiber-optic cable in New Jersey by a construction crew. DECADES-OLD COMPUTERS AND SPARE PARTS FROM EBAY The FAA relies on telecoms systems it is racing to replace as well as decades-old Compaq computers and replacement parts bought on eBay. The US has the world's most complex airspace and faces a shortage of several thousand air traffic controllers. The country's air traffic facilities cannot talk to one another and operate on individual analog computers. "Every facility is a silo," Bedford told Reuters in a recent interview. The FAA has also been working for years to end a long-ridiculed, decades-old practice of air traffic controllers using paper flight strips to keep track of aircraft. But adopting the change, which started in 2022, at 49 major airports will take until at least 2028. A total of 27 major airports have already done away with the paper strips.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON, Nov 5 : The United States is warning of an "ongoing cyber threat" to industrial refrigeration systems, saying in a statement issued Thursday that every organization that depends on cold storage should assume it could fall into the hackers' crosshairs. The statement said that unidentified "malicious cyber actors" were targeting vulnerabilities in internet-accessible electronic temperature and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities. "If successfully exploited, the actors could change the temperature and possibly cause physical impacts such as fire hazards, loss of inventory and changes to the service life of the system," said the statement, which was issued by the FBI, the cyber defense agency CISA, and other government departments. "Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target," said Chris Butera, CISA's acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity.

Source: Reuters

Nov 5 : The Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, Wall Street's industry regulator, said on Thursday it fined Webull Financial $4.2 million for failing to implement programs aimed at preventing illicit finance and other issues. • Between January 2020 and September 2023, the digital brokerage did not implement reasonably designed programs to prevent money laundering and identity theft, FINRA said. • The firm did not have reasonable policies in place, for example, to verify customer identities when they signed up for accounts, FINRA said. • Webull also did not establish policies and procedures to detect and flag suspicious transactions, FINRA said. • The firm also failed to institute a program to make sure customer transactions were done in the best way for the customers, FINRA said. • Webull, which did not admit or deny FINRA's findings, did not respond immediately to requests for comment. • As part of the settlement, Webull has agreed to remediate issues and hire an independent consultant.

Source: Reuters

Nov 5 : LIV Golf, which shook up world golf in 2022, will liquidate after losing big-name players and the financing it needed to stay alive, the breakaway circuit said on Thursday. Throughout the wind-down process, LIV Golf said it would remain open to, and continue to consider any offers from third parties that could get more value from its assets. "In light of the current circumstances, we believe shifting toward an orderly wind-down is the most responsible path forward for the League at this time," Gene Davis and Jon Zinman of LIV Golf board’s special committee said in a press release. LIV Golf had secured $300 million of potential financing from BC Partners to allow the staging of tournaments in 2027 but scrapped the plan after a number of notable players opted not to commit to the league.

The future of LIV Golf had been in question after the circuit lost financial support from the deep-pocketed Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund beyond the now-completed 2026 season. Leading golfers like former world number one Jon Rahm announced their departures from LIV Golf after it filed for bankruptcy protection in September. LIV Golf sent shockwaves through the sport when it burst onto the scene in June 2022 with a mix of star power and past-their-prime veterans who signed lucrative contracts to appear in tournaments with guaranteed paydays. MAJOR CHAMPIONS The PGA Tour refused to let members compete in LIV Golf events, and suspended defecting golfers who included major champions like Bryson DeChambeau, Dustin Johnson, Brooks Koepka and Phil Mickelson. Those suspensions triggered a wave of bitter legal battles, including an antitrust lawsuit in which DeChambeau, Mickelson and others accused the PGA Tour of using monopoly power to penalize independent contractors. Critics decried LIV Golf as a vehicle for Saudi Arabia to improve its reputation and deflect criticism of its human rights record. The Saudi government denies accusations of human rights abuses. In June 2023, the PGA Tour and the Saudi fund again stunned the world of golf by announcing a framework to form one unified commercial entity, and end the litigation. As talks stalled, the PGA Tour even enlisted Donald Trump in the hope the US president, an avid golfer whose courses have hosted multiple LIV events, could broker a deal. The PGA Tour ultimately rejected the Saudi fund's offer to invest $1.5 billion on condition that LIV Golf would remain intact and fund governor Yasir Al-Rumayyan would co-chair the PGA Tour Enterprises' board. In late April, after pouring more than $5 billion into LIV Golf, the Saudi fund said the circuit no longer fitted its investment strategy, and it would pull funding after the 2026 season. "Building a global platform designed to bring new, younger, and more diverse fans to the sport of golf has been the round of a lifetime for all of us," LIV Golf CEO Scott O’Neil said. "LIV Golf was fun, demanding, inspiring, at times challenging — but always rewarding."

Source: Reuters

Nov 5 : Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin has delayed its New Glenn rocket launch into January 2027 after a major explosion forced delays earlier this year, two people familiar with the matter said on Thursday, citing an email sent by CEO Dave Limp to employees. Blue Origin did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. New Glenn, Blue Origin's flagship heavy-lift orbital rocket, has been grounded since exploding on the company's only launchpad in May, days before the planned launch of Amazon satellites.  The explosion badly damaged the Florida launchpad, where the 30-storey-tall (322 feet) rocket had lifted off three times since its 2025 debut. The company is now targeting January for its next launch after facing a series of delays reconstructing the launchpad in Florida, according to Limp's email on Wednesday, the sources said. The Financial Times first reported the news on Thursday.

LONDON: Ukraine's renewed attacks on Russian oil refineries add to Moscow's difficulty in addressing domestic fuel shortages while it ships diesel to international markets under an export deal with US President Donald Trump. The Ryazan oil refinery , one of R us sia's largest, appeared to have come under attack as part of a large drone strike overnight on ind us trial sites in the city, southeast of Moscow, according to a Reuters video analysis. If confirmed, it would be the second refinery to be hit this week following an attack on the Yaroslavl plant, northeast of Moscow, overnight on Monday (Nov 2), marking the breakdown of a pa us e in strikes. Ukraine's strikes on oil refineries this year forced large amounts of processing capacity in western R us sia offline, ca us ing fuel shortages that meant Moscow had to enforce fuel export bans from April onwards.

A ban on diesel exports has been lifted in part and the US struck the deal in October with the Kremlin to resume diesel exports to international markets when Trump was seeking to calm diesel prices ahead of the midterm elections on Nov 3, which Trump's Republican Party lost . The city of Ryazan had restored power supply earlier on Thursday as fires at the unnamed ind us trial sites were either contained or put out, the local governor said on social media.

US -R US SIA DIESEL CARGOES ARE IN FOC US At least six Russian diesel cargoes have broadcast that they plan transatlantic voyages, shipping data from Kpler and LSEG show, while two cargoes appeared to have changed course after being previo us ly bound for the US Atlantic coast. No Russian diesel cargo has arrived in the US since the deal , the data show. The first observed US -bound Russian shipment is expected to arrive in New York this weekend, but regulatory, legislative and sanctions concerns mean that its discharge is not guaranteed, Kpler analyst Matt Smith said. "These are commercial loadings, so naturally the details cannot be made public. All the diesel will find its buyers," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on a daily conference call. Tankers often broadcast messages known as signals, such as "ATLANTIC COAST FOR ORDERS," indicating they are heading for the US Atlantic coast but have no confirmed discharge port, so the crew is awaiting instructions. Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Russian diesel cargoes destined for the US are continuing on course, in a post on X. There is no connection between diesel tankers changing course and the result of the US midterm elections, Peskov added.

FAST

NEW YORK, Nov 5 : Tech stocks were headed for their worst decline since June on Thursday, with the semiconductor index briefly falling by double digits in the latest autumn reckoning for the AI sector. The SOX fell as much as 11 per cent, its worst performance since March 2020, and the Nasdaq composite dropped as much as 5 per cent, a decline that would confirm a correction denoting a 10 per cent pullback from its high last month. Advanced Micro, Sandisk, Micron, Dell and Marvell Technology were among the more than a dozen large technology stocks down by double digits percentagewise.  It's the latest in a string of selloffs for the AI sector in what has been a bruising month since the Nasdaq's record close on October 6. Selling in stock and bond markets has reduced access to financing for many participants in the data-center buildout, while Tuesday's US elections brought the passage of dozens of nationwide ballot initiatives that stand to limit building in coming months and years.

COMMENTS: ADAM SARHAN, CHIEF EXECUTIVE OF 50 PARK INVESTMENTS IN NEW YORK "AI stocks are already in a private bear market that virtually nobody is talking about. If you look at the semiconductor index, it's down about 31 per cent from its 52-week high. The point is that many AI-related stocks are already deep into bear market territory, and very few people are discussing it."We're seeing large companies such as Apple cut back on AI spending because they are not seeing sufficient return on investment. The hype around AI was enormous, but now the market is asking whether customers will continue paying for these products and services. "I'm not using AI as much as I was six or twelve months ago, and I'm definitely not spending as much on it. As that revenue starts to dry up, investors are asking what the next bullish catalyst is. Right now, there doesn't appear to be a clear answer. In short, we're seeing the unwinding of the AI trade, while big technology stocks are moving deeper into correction territory."Looking ahead, there's a strong possibility of a significant policy shift in Washington. Different policies could create new winners and losers across sectors." WILL COMPERNOLLE, MACRO STRATEGIST, FHN FINANCIAL, CHICAGO: “It's really tempting to overinterpret or over extrapolate the first few hours of moves yesterday morning, but we already see that people continue to digest it, and they're all moving targets. Some of the narratives that seemed to be dominating yesterday reversed very quickly and we're still waiting for the dust to settle. It does look like there is this shift away from chipmaker stocks that is causing a bid for Treasuries. “Everything is tied to AI right now. The biggest market moves in October were, relatively speaking, pretty small tweaks in AI sentiment. But that is the catalyst. That is what determines demand for credit, economic growth, so many different things and I think after the midterms, a big question is how the outcome affects the trajectory of AI investment and we've already seen that rotation out of chip stocks and into hyperscalers. I think that shows that there are expectations for slower investment, but that could increase the viability of the hyperscalers, which seem to be in the middle of a kind of frenzied race to the bottom or top, depending on how you look at it. “I don't think there's been a bigger impact on Treasuries because it could be that people are already pricing this in, not only a Democratic sweep, but also, you know, Greg Abbott, I think last year, the current governor of Texas, said that he used to be a huge advocate for data centers and he wanted Texas to be the capital of it all and he imposed a moratorium on new permits in September. And to me, that reflects how the political environment already signaled a backlash regardless. "This week's results kind of codify it or underscore what was already happening, which is that people don't want these things in their backyard. Whether it's their understanding or misunderstanding of data centers’ impacts is beside the point. I think there's so much political pressure right now to slow down AI data centers and I think that is potentially the biggest driver of rates over the next couple of months.” PETER ANDERSEN, FOUNDER OF ANDERSEN CAPITAL MANAGEMENT IN BOSTON: “I think the sell-off first is unwarranted. And secondly, it's just the investors reorganizing their thoughts around the election results and how much policies will change to artificial intelligence and the associated technologies with that, such as the data center build outs. We've seen a lot of talk about delaying or moratoriums on certain states will not allow the data centers to be built. Investors are just trying to grapple with all that.” “It's going to take a while before investors actually get a clear picture. The election was yesterday, and it certainly will take some time to sink in as a general message and what the direction will be. So, for instance, I can see this as having a minimal impact. Say the data centers are not allowed to be built in the majority states of the United States. Our due diligence and interviewing with people that work in the data center construction have said they don't care. They'll go to Canada or Brazil, for instance. Brazil is calling asking if they can host these data centers. So there are certainly clear workarounds. The general investor has the enlightenment yet about what the alternatives are and there will be plenty of workarounds.” BRUCE ZARO, MANAGING DIRECTOR AT GRANITE WEALTH MANAGEMENT IN PLYMOUTH, MASSACHUSETTS: "It is really is kind of a secondary reaction to yesterday's election results... Yesterday's enthusiasm, in my view, was much less about who won or who lost, but the fact that we're now past that and we're looking through the windshield rather than the rearview mirror.  "Today, there's been a revisitation of that enthusiasm. And basically the semiconductors and the data center stocks are under immense pressure and all their ecosystems around them, because there's going to be a lot of pushback. "There's going to be a lot of pushback about those data centers being geographically located in someone's backyard, straining the power grid, straining the water systems. And so, although there are a number of data centers already approved, there are still a lot to be permitted. There's going to be a difficult road to get those permitted forthcoming. So I think that's what today's sell off is about." MARK HACKETT, CHIEF MARKET STRATEGIST FOR NATIONWIDE, DOWNINGTOWN, PENNSYLVANIA:"What is being blamed is relatively weak earnings from Qualcomm and ARM Holdings. That was a reminder that the fundamentals still matter but also the election likely putting a governor on the speed of the AI build out, that is particularly impactful to the semiconductor space and the neo-cloud space - the kind of more speculative areas of the tech market. "They're dragging pretty much everything else down. But the main driver here is very aggressive institutional selling and de-leveraging by hedge funds and more active institutional managers. Today, this is an emotional sell-off." MELISSA BROWN, GLOBAL HEAD OF INVESTMENT DECISION RESEARCH AT SIMCORP, NEW YORK: "Investors appear to be recognizing that some newly elected members of Congress and governors are looking to slow the pace of AI infrastructure development. While it seems unlikely that they will be able to stop it altogether, any slowdown would raise concerns because the AI growth story has largely depended on the rapid buildout of supporting infrastructure. That could create uncertainty for many companies exposed to the sector, at least in the near to medium term." SAMEER SAMANA, SENIOR GLOBAL MARKET STRATEGIST, WELLS FARGO INVESTMENT INSTITUTE, ST. LOUIS, MISSOURI: "What the market's focused on is that they priced in quite a bit of growth. And if that growth slows, then I think you have to switch from one investor base to a new investor base. The initial investor base was all about growth. They're going to move on somewhere else. The new investor base is the one who has to say, all right, I want healthy cash flow companies. Those are two different investor bases. Anything related to AI is down more than anything not related to AI. That handoff from growth investors to value investors may take some time because a lot of these stocks aren't exactly cheap yet. "Thematically, if AI is where growth has to be kind of moderated, that's probably where investors have to mark down their expectations and some may choose to exit entirely. "Yesterday was all about just we're all programmed to buy the dip. And when people saw that stock futures were selling off overnight last night, there's just now always a knee-jerk reaction to buy any dip. And because it's rewarded time and again by the market going higher like it did yesterday. The question is are there more dip buyers or are there more longer term investors for whom the story is meaningfully changing? And so yesterday, you can chalk one up to for the dip buyers, but today the long-term investors are the ones that are more meaningful." IPEK OZKARDESKAYA, SENIOR ANALYST AT SWISSQUOTE BANK, GENEVA, SWITZERLAND: "What we see in technology today is basically the unwinding of the AI trade if you look at the broader picture. Coming into this earnings season, there were worries that AI spending was too much. Those worries were already interfering with stronger-than-expected results from technology companies and strong results failed to improve appetite among tech investors. "We were already in a market mood that was not very appetising for technology due to the huge spending, higher borrowing costs and the fact that free cash flow levels at these hyperscalers are falling right now. They are issuing more equity and more bonds in order to finance additional AI spending, and both more equity and more bonds are negative for valuations. We were coming into this week and into the midterms with this sentiment already in place, and then the midterms were basically the last nail in the coffin.""There is now a chance that the two years of extra push from the Trump government for AI buildout will somehow be scaled back because there has been a lot about the AI trade that has been ignored by the current administration, whether we are talking about the impact on jobs, the economy or the environment. We suspect there is going to be some scrutiny on this aggressive AI buildout. "The fact that hyperscalers rallied yesterday on the possibility of an AI slowdown was actually interesting, as investors thought that if companies cannot slow down, maybe the government will slow them down. But these companies have spent so much money and put so much of their weight behind AI that a slowdown story may also come back and bite the hyperscalers. Many of these hyperscalers are also in the data-centre business, so they are very much tied to AI adoption and the fact that AI adoption accelerates."Looking at the market right now, we see that political worries are mounting and they are only adding to the previous worries that we already had in the sector. This is creating some panic and stress in the market right now, especially when you think that valuations were quite tight going into the earnings season. Strong earnings did not help and politics are not helping either. It is one more risk factor that comes and adds to the long list of things that could go wrong with the current pace of AI buildout."

Source: Reuters

NEW YORK, Nov 5 : Global stocks fell on Thursday, weighed down by a sharp selloff in semiconductor shares after weak earnings from Qualcomm and concerns that a Democrat-controlled US Congress could slow investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure. Wall Street's main indexes tumbled, with the Nasdaq on track to confirm a correction from its record closing high. Technology stocks led declines among S&P 500 sectors, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index slumped 11 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 2.2 per cent, the S&P 500 slid 3.4 per cent, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.2 per cent. Qualcomm shares dived 11 per cent after the company's smartphone chip sales missed Wall Street estimates.

"Disappointing earnings and the Dem sweep potentially slowing the AI buildout are pressing sentiment," said Mark Hackett, chief market strategist at Nationwide. "This is a volatile and cyclical group, and when sentiment shifts, the reactions are intense." Candidates in Tuesday's midterm elections who opposed data centre expansion and campaigned in part on moratoriums on new developments also secured victories in Texas and Georgia, adding to concerns about the outlook for AI-related infrastructure spending. The MSCI All-World index fell 2.5 per cent, having surrendered earlier gains, while Europe's STOXX 600 lost 0.67 per cent. "Hedge funds have been aggressively selling for weeks in this area. They were caught short yesterday and were forced to cover but today is a reflection that their bias is still to be short or to de-lever in the semiconductors and neoclouds," Hackett said. OIL REVERSES COURSE Brent crude futures was last up 2.58 per cent on the day, at $97 a barrel, as investors refocused on uncertainties about the future course of the US war with Iran. After Trump's Republican Party suffered heavy losses in the midterm elections on Tuesday, oil prices had tumbled. Trump acknowledged on Wednesday that the war played a role in Republicans' defeat and his vice president, JD Vance, was even more blunt on X: "The reason we lost is the war."  Bond prices eased from the day's highs, in line with the rebound in the crude price, leaving yields on benchmark 10-year US notes down 1.22 basis points on the day at 4.88 per cent.  In currencies, the dollar edged into positive territory, gaining on the euro, which held at $1.1222, and against the pound, which held at $1.3466 after the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 and signalled more may be necessary if the Iran war continues. Gold traded above $4,100 an ounce, having risen 5 per cent in two days, its largest two-day jump since early April.

Nov 5 : India's opening one-day international against Sri Lanka on December 13 has been moved from Delhi to Visakhapatnam after the Delhi and District Cricket Association asked for a venue change, the Board of Control for Cricket in India said on Thursday. The BCCI said the DDCA cited "potential weather disruption and the proposed renovation work at the (Arun Jaitley) stadium" as reasons for seeking the switch. The match would have been the capital's first ODI since the 2023 World Cup. It will now be held at the ACA-VDCA Cricket Stadium in Visakhapatnam. According to Cricbuzz, the concerns raised by the DDCA are also linked to Delhi's air quality during December, with officials keen to avoid a repeat of the issues during India's test match versus Sri Lanka in 2017.

Fireworks during the Hindu festival of Diwali, which falls on November 8 this year, worsen the pollution in India. TOLEDO, Spain, Nov 5 : Family, friends and teammates gathered in the village of Navahermosa on Thursday for the funeral of Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel, who died following an on-field collision. De Miguel collided with Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono during Monday's match and was taken to intensive care. Tenerife confirmed De Miguel's death on Tuesday morning. The Tenerife squad, club staff and majority shareholder Rayco Garcia attended the funeral, along with Royal Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) President Rafael Louzan, Spain coach Luis de la Fuente, Real Madrid President Florentino Perez and Atletico Madrid CEO Miguel Angel Gil Marin. De Miguel's coffin was carried out of San Miguel Arcangel church in a procession to the cemetery.

De Miguel's family thanked well-wishers for their support in a statement read by his agent Manuel Hernandez before the funeral. "Feeling so much affection for Jesus and seeing the impact he had on so many people is something we will always carry with us," the family said in the statement read by Hernandez. "Jesus leaves a void that is impossible to fill, but also cherished memories for all of us who were fortunate enough to share our lives with him. Thank you for loving him and for standing by us." Spanish police have opened a routine investigation into De Miguel's death. Andorra released a statement on Wednesday, in which Owono said: "These are the most difficult days of my life." Tenerife's match against Granada and Andorra's game with Mallorca, both scheduled for this weekend, have been postponed. Tenerife's main rivals, Las Palmas, will play their fixture against Eldense on Sunday in blue and white colours, traditionally worn by Tenerife, as a tribute to De Miguel. Garcia invited fans to Tenerife's stadium on Saturday to pay their respects to De Miguel in what he called 'the last goodbye'. LALIGA TO GO AHEAD The Spanish Footballers’ Association said on Thursday it had requested the suspension of this weekend's round of matches. LaLiga later confirmed that fixtures in the first and second divisions would go ahead, with the exception of Andorra-Mallorca, Granada-Tenerife and Castellon-Eibar. De Miguel spent two-and-a-half years at Castellon before moving to Tenerife in 2025, and LaLiga accepted the club's request to postpone their match. A minute's silence will be observed before each game that goes ahead, while the referee will stop play at the first interruption after the ninth minute, in recognition of the number nine shirt De Miguel wore for Tenerife. The tributes were agreed by LaLiga, Liga F, the RFEF, players and clubs.

Source: Reuters

Nov 5 : The Nasdaq slid more than 10 per cent from its record close on Thursday, on track to confirm a correction as worries over massive AI spending and heightened scrutiny of data-center expansion rattled tech stocks. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index fell nearly 4 per cent to 24,712.60, more than 10 per cent below its record closing high of 27,599.89 reached on October 6. Thursday's slide erased the previous session's gains after Democrats swept both houses of Congress, as investors weighed the prospect of greater scrutiny of further AI infrastructure buildout. "When you go from full unified control under one party to full unified control under another party that can also represent quite a bit of uncertainty, discontinuity and abrupt change to policy," said Sameer Samana, senior global market strategist at Wells Fargo Investment Institute.

"When it looked like the Democrats were going to take significant majorities in both the House and the Senate, we thought that at the very least, it would lead to markets taking a little bit of a pause." A decline of 10 per cent from the most recent record closing high is widely considered a correction. It would mark the Nasdaq's second correction this year. Sentiment toward AI-linked stocks has deteriorated in recent weeks, with the Nasdaq shedding more than $2.5 trillion in market value in October. Several big tech companies are tapping debt markets to help finance billions of dollars in planned investments in data centers, chips and other infrastructure required to support AI development. Investors have increasingly questioned how quickly those investments will translate into profits, particularly as persistent geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and fears of prolonged inflation have kept borrowing costs elevated. Earnings from hyperscalers Alphabet and Meta last month failed to reassure investors about the returns on AI spending, contributing to a broader selloff in AI-linked stocks.
